senses.definition: A light blow or jolting collision.
examples: His car had a tiny bump with a moving bus.

senses.definition: The sound of such a collision.
examples: He heard a loud bump and saw the front part of his car was broken and the driver of the other car was running to apologise.

senses.definition: A protuberance on a level surface.
A swelling on the skin caused by illness or injury.

quotes.text: It had upon its brow / A bump as big as a young cockerel's stone.
quotes.reference: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:

senses.definition: (obsolete) One of the protuberances on the cranium which, in phrenology, are associated with distinct faculties or affections of the mind. Also (dated, metonymic) the faculty itself
examples: the bump of veneration; the bump of acquisitiveness
Our task is to elevate the character of the people, raising up, in fact, their bump of self-esteem and suppressing the bumps of servility and fury.

quotes.text: Another, with the bump of order unnaturally developed, had his folios and quartos all reduced, in binding, to one size, so that they might look even on his bookshelves.
quotes.reference: 1902, William Blades, The Enemies of Books, 2nd edition, page 102:

senses.definition: (rowing) The point, in a race in which boats are spaced apart at the start, at which a boat begins to overtake the boat ahead.
The swollen abdomen of a pregnant woman.
(Internet) A post in an Internet forum thread made in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.
A temporary increase in a quantity, as shown in a graph.
examples: US presidential nominees get a post-convention bump in survey ratings.

senses.definition: (slang) A dose of a drug such as ketamine or cocaine, when snorted recreationally.

quotes.text: “They're getting their drugs mixed up,” she said. “If someone did a line of coke, it would be a very different size than if someone did a bump of ketamine, right? So if they're thinking it's cocaine and they do a line, they could go into a k-hole and be completely unable to move for hours. Maybe not hours, but for a while.”

quotes.text: We sing […] "God Save the Queen" done in mime and finally "Clap Hands, Here Comes Charley" to a Hawaiian rock with Phoebe doing the bump.
quotes.reference: 1979, Robert English, Toxic Kisses, Eden Paperbacks, page 32:

senses.definition: In skipping, a single jump over two consecutive turns of the rope.
(uncountable) A coarse cotton fabric.
A training match for a fighting dog.
(snooker, slang) The jaw of either of the middle pockets.
(US, slang, uncountable) Music, especially played over speakers at loud volume with strong bass frequency response.

quotes.text: Call me the juice and you know I'm a stunt; ride in the car with some bump in the trunk.

senses.definition: (US, broadcasting) A short, self-promotional spot on a radio or television station.
(industrial relations) A reassignment of jobs within an organization (for example, when an existing employee leaves) on the basis of seniority.

quotes.text: For example, chain bumping, in which a bump by one employee initiates a series of consecutive bumps down a progression line before a layoff results, produces the greatest average number of reassignments per redundant employee.

(colloquial) A minor problem or difficulty.

quotes.text: "I'll try my best, but we still have a few bumps to work out," Ryder muttered.

senses.definition: (mining) A sudden movement of underground strata, preceded by a characteristic sound.
To knock against or run into with a jolt.
examples: Their car got bumped while they were turning at the junction.

senses.definition: To move up or down by a step; displace.
examples: I bumped the font size up to make my document easier to read.

senses.definition: (Internet) To post in an Internet forum thread in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.

quotes.text: As in [the online forum] carersvoicesnz, certain contributors were more visible, taking the initiative to "bump" the thread to bring it back into view if it went quiet.
quotes.reference: 2015, Barbara Horrell, Christine Stephens, Mary Breheny, “Online Research with Informal Caregivers: Opportunities and Challenges”, in Qualitative Research in Psychology, volume 12, number 3, →DOI, page 264:

senses.definition: (physical chemistry, of a superheated liquid) To suddenly boil, causing movement of the vessel and loss of liquid.

quotes.text: Heat until the liquid bumps, then reduce the heat and continue the boiling for 1½ hours.

senses.definition: (transitive) To move (a booked passenger) to a later flight because of earlier delays or cancellations.

quotes.text: Easyjet said the compensation package for passengers bumped off flights was 'probably the most flawed piece of European legislation in recent years' […]
quotes.reference: 2005, Lois Jones, EasyJet: the story of Britain's biggest low-cost airline, page 192:

senses.definition: (transitive) To move the time of (a scheduled event).

quotes.text: A colleague emails with news that her 4:30 meeting got bumped to 3:30.

senses.definition: (transitive) To pick (a lock) with a repeated striking motion that dislodges the pins.
(transitive, programming) To increase (a version number).
(intransitive, archaic) To make a loud, heavy, or hollow noise; to boom.

senses.definition: (printing, dated) To spread out material so as to fill any desired number of pages.
(slang, transitive) To assassinate; to bump off.
examples: You know about the night the kid bumped Brody?

senses.definition: (industrial relations, transitive) To displace (another employee in an organization) on the basis of seniority.

quotes.text: Employees with 2 years or more, and less than 8 years plant seniority, may bump a probationary employee.

senses.definition: (colloquial, dated) To anger, irritate.

quotes.text: After his ancestors had been browbeaten by the Puritans, and his ancestors had been driven out by the early pioneers [...], if he learned that a magnificent bronze statue is to be erected to his ancestors; wouldn't it bump an Indian?

(criminal slang and US military slang, circa 1920–1950) To encounter and stop, to catch.
(intransitive) To move while bumping up and down, as a cart or car does on rough ground.
examples: The car bumped over the dirt road.
